title: What a chart is for
summary: A chart answers one question for one audience with one message. Decide those first, write the message as the title, and know when a table does the job better.
objectives: Say the question a chart answers, who it is for and the one message it carries.
Tell a chart made to explore data from one made to explain it.
Write a title that states the finding, not the topic.
Decide when a table serves the reader better than a chart.

slides.h: A table makes you read; a chart makes you see
p: The same five numbers, two ways. In a table you compare 3,682.2 with 3,122.4 digit by digit. In a chart the pattern jumps out before you read a single number.
A chart turns numbers into lengths, positions and colours, which the eye compares instantly.
It shows **patterns**: the biggest, the smallest, the gap, the trend.
It hides **exact values**, unless you label them.
In real life: used to send the regional heads a table every month. Nobody replied. The first month she sent this chart, the East head called her within the hour.

p: Before you pick a chart, answer three things: what question it answers, who will read it, and the **one sentence** you want them to remember.
The ops head deciding where to send help needs a different chart from the finance team checking totals.
If you can’t say the message in one sentence, you’re not ready to chart it.
One chart, one message. Two messages? Two charts.
In real life: asked for “a chart of sales”. Asked what he’d decide with it, he said: “which stores get the extra Diwali staff”. The right chart was revenue per store in October, not sales by month.

p: Some charts are for **you**, to understand the data: quick, many, default settings. Others are for **someone else**: one message each, designed so it lands.
Explore freely: try a bar, a line, a scatter, and throw most away.
Explain sparingly: send the one chart that answers the question.
This course is mostly about **explaining** charts, the ones other people see.
In real life: made 30 charts while studying a year of shipments. Her report to the directors had three.

p: A title like “Revenue by region” names the **topic**. A title like “South brings 30% of revenue; East and Central lag” states the **finding**. Readers remember titles.
Write the title as a short sentence: subject and what it did.
Put units and the period in a subtitle or the axis, not the title.
If the finding changes next month, the title changes too. Module 4 makes titles update themselves.
In real life: has one rule for slides: a reader who sees only the titles should get the whole story. Their charts are titled “Costs rose 12% while sales fell”, never “Costs and sales”.

slides.h: When a table beats a chart
p: Charts show patterns. When the reader needs **exact values** to look up, or there are only two or three numbers, a table is better.
Two numbers? Write a sentence: “Sales rose from ₹112 crore to ₹122 crore.”
A table can still guide the eye: bold the key row, shade one column.
Module 5 puts small visuals **inside** tables: data bars, icons, sparklines.
In real life: asked a client to replace a pie chart of 40 expense heads with a table. “I need to tick each one,” she said. “I can’t tick a slice.”

p: Show your chart to someone for five seconds, then hide it. Can they tell you the message? If not, the chart isn’t finished.
Most readers give a chart a few seconds before they move on.
If they mention a detail instead of the message, cut or grey the detail.
Lesson 1.3 is all about the cutting.
In real life: starts with every regional head looking at the same chart for five seconds. The CEO then asks one person to say what it shows. The analysts design for that moment.

demo.intro: Chart Tulsi Mart’s revenue by region in Excel, then give it a title that says the finding.

frames.say: Select **A1:B6**: the regions and their revenue, with the heading row but **not the Total row**. Then click **Insert › Recommended Charts**.

callouts.text: Excel suggests charts for your data

frames.say: For five categories Excel suggests a **Clustered Column** chart. Click **OK**. (Alt+F1 inserts the default chart in one keystroke.)
The chart lands on the sheet with a placeholder, **Chart Title**. That’s not a title yet.
Click the title and type the **finding**: South brings 30% of revenue; East and Central lag. Now the chart says something.

lab.intro: Tulsi Mart’s revenue by region for FY 2025-26 is in **A1:C7**, in ₹ lakh. Ravi, the head of operations, asks: **“Which regions need help?”** Find the message, then chart it with the chart builder under each task.

tasks.explain: It answers his question with a finding he can act on: East and Central lag.

quiz.q: What should you settle before choosing a chart type?
options: The question, the audience and the one message
quiz.explain: The chart type follows from the question and the message.

options: Sales peaked in October and dipped in July

quiz.q: You select A1:B7, including the Total row, and insert a column chart. What do you see?
options: Six bars, with a Total bar towering over the regions
quiz.explain: The total becomes a sixth category and squashes the rest. Leave totals out of the chart’s data.

quiz.q: An auditor needs every store’s revenue to the rupee. What do you give her?
quiz.explain: Exact values to look up: a table.

options: Made in seconds with default settings
Designed for someone else, with one message
quiz.explain: Explaining charts are designed for a reader.

quiz.q: What does the five-second test check?
options: That a reader can say the message after seeing it for five seconds

points: Decide the **question**, the **audience** and the **one message** before the chart.
**Explore** with many quick charts; **explain** with one designed chart per message.
The **title states the finding**; a **table** wins when readers need exact values.
recap.cheat: Question → audience → one message → chart; the title states the finding.

cards.front: Three things to decide before choosing a chart
Topic title or finding title: “Revenue by region”

**Exploring**: quick, many, for you. **Explaining**: designed, one message, for someone else.

cards.back: When readers need **exact values**, there are only two or three numbers, or the units differ.

cards.back: No: it becomes one more bar that towers over the parts.
